633-623-644|maq|0: Sīn, hamza and lām form a single word. One says saʾala, yasʾalu, suʾālan and masʾalatan [to ask]. A man who is suʾala asks a great deal.
633-623-644|muf|0: al-Suʾāl (asking) is calling for knowledge, or for what leads to knowledge, and calling for wealth, or what leads to wealth. A request for knowledge is answered by the tongue, with the hand standing in for it by writing or gesture; a request for wealth is answered by the hand, with the tongue standing in for it by a promise or a refusal. If it is said: how can asking be for knowledge, when it is known that Allah the Exalted asks His servants, as in “And when Allah said: O ʿĪsā son of Maryam” [al-Māʾida 116]? It is answered: that is asking in order to make the people know, and to rebuke them — not so that Allah may know, for He is the Knower of the unseen. So it does not cease to be asking about knowledge. Asking for knowledge is sometimes to find something out and sometimes to rebuke, as in His saying: “And when the girl buried alive is asked” [al-Takwīr 8] — so that the one asked may come to know.
633-623-644|muf|1: When asking is for information, it takes its second object sometimes directly and sometimes with a preposition. You say: I asked him such-and-such, and I asked him about (ʿan) such-and-such, and with bi — and with ʿan more often: “They ask you about the Spirit” [al-Isrāʾ 85], “They ask you about Dhū al-Qarnayn” [al-Kahf 83], “They ask you about the spoils” [al-Anfāl 1]; and He said: “And when My servants ask you about Me” [al-Baqara 186]; and: “A questioner asked about a punishment bound to fall” [al-Maʿārij 1]. When asking is a request for wealth, it takes its object directly
633-623-644|muf|2: or with min, as in: “And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen” [al-Aḥzāb 53], “Ask for what you spent, and let them ask for what they spent” [al-Mumtaḥana 10], and He said: “And ask Allah of His bounty” [al-Nisāʾ 32]. The poor person, when asking for something, is called al-sāʾil, as in: “And as for the one who asks, do not repel him” [al-Ḍuḥā 10], and His saying: “for the one who asks and the one deprived” [al-Dhāriyāt 19].
633-623-644|lis|0: Saʾala, yasʾalu, suʾālan, saʾālatan, masʾalatan, tasʾālan and saʾlatan [all: to ask]. Abū Dhuʾayb said:
633-623-644|lis|1: [Poetry:] “Did you question the traces of the abode, or did you not ask — about its dwellers, or about how long since they were there?”
633-623-644|lis|2: One says saʾaltu, asʾalu and also saltu, asalu [the same without hamza]; two men yatasāʾalān and yatasāyalān [ask each other]. The plural of masʾala is masāʾil, with hamza; when they drop the hamza they say masala. Tasāʾalū: some of them asked others. In the Glorious Revelation: “And fear Allah, through whom you ask one another (tasāʾalūna), and the ties of kinship” — and it is also read tasāʾalūna [with the hamza softened].
646-628-623|maq|0: Nūn, bāʾ and hamza: its measure is coming from one place to another. One who comes from one land to another is called nābiʾ. A nābiʾ torrent is one that comes from one country to another, and a nābiʾ man likewise. [The poet] said:
646-628-623|maq|1: [Poetry:] “But what clouded it was every dishevelled stranger who came (nābiʾ), whom fate brought to us from where we do not know.”
646-628-623|maq|2: From this same measure is al-nabaʾ, news, because it comes from one place to another. The munbiʾ is the one who informs. Anbaʾtuhu and nabbaʾtuhu [I informed him]. A marksman shot and anbaʾa when he did not graze [the target], as though his arrow turned away from scratching it and fell somewhere else. al-Nabʾa is a sound — and this is the measure, because a sound comes from one place to another. Dhū al-Rumma said:
646-628-623|maq|3: [Poetry, describing a wild animal:] “It sensed a faint sound — the one in the empty land is keen — through the nabʾa of a voice; there is no falsehood in its hearing.”
646-628-623|maq|4: Those who pronounce al-nabīʾ (the Prophet) with hamza do so because he brought news (anbaʾa) from Allah the Exalted. And Allah knows best what is right.
646-628-623|muf|0: al-Nabaʾ is news of great benefit through which knowledge, or a strong presumption, is gained. News is not originally called nabaʾ until
646-628-623|muf|1: it contains these three things [great benefit, knowledge or strong presumption]. News that is called nabaʾ should be free of falsehood, like mass-transmitted (mutawātir) reports, the news of Allah the Exalted, and the news of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Because nabaʾ includes the sense of khabar (report), one says anbaʾtuhu bi-kadhā, as you say akhbartuhu bi-kadhā [I told him of such]; and because it includes the sense of knowledge, one says anbaʾtuhu kadhā, as you say aʿlamtuhu kadhā [I made him know such]. Allah the Exalted said: “Say: It is great news (nabaʾ) from which you turn away” [Ṣād 67–68], and He said: “About what are they asking one another? About the great news (al-nabaʾ al-ʿaẓīm)” [al-Nabaʾ 1–2]; “Has there not come to you the news of those who disbelieved before, so they tasted the evil result of their affair?” [al-Taghābun 5]; and He said: “That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you” [Hūd 49]; and He said:
646-628-623|muf|2: “Those cities — We relate to you some of their news” [al-Aʿrāf 101]; and He said: “That is from the news of the cities which We relate to you” [Hūd 100]; and His saying:
646-628-623|muf|3: “If a wrongdoer comes to you with news (nabaʾ), verify it” [al-Ḥujurāt 6] — this is a warning that when a report concerns something great and weighty, it deserves to be paused over, even if it is known and its truth is likely, until it is looked into again and made fully clear. One says:
646-628-623|muf|4: nabbaʾtuhu and anbaʾtuhu. Allah the Exalted said: “Inform me (anbiʾūnī) of the names of these, if you are truthful” [al-Baqara 31], and He said:
646-628-623|muf|5: “Inform them of their names. And when he had informed them of their names” [al-Baqara 33], and He said: “I will inform you (nabbaʾtukumā) of its interpretation” [Yūsuf 37], “And inform them about the guests of Ibrāhīm” [al-Ḥijr 51], and He said: “Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on earth?” [Yūnus 18], “Say: Name them! Or do you inform Him of what He does not know?” [al-Raʿd 33], and He said: “Inform me with knowledge if you are truthful” [al-Anʿām 143], “Allah has already informed us of your news” [al-Tawba 94]. Nabbaʾtuhu is more emphatic than anbaʾtuhu: “We will surely inform (fa-la-nunabbiʾanna) those who disbelieved” [Fuṣṣilat 50], “Man will be informed (yunabbaʾu) that Day of what he sent forward and what he left behind” [al-Qiyāma 13]. This is shown by His saying: “When he informed her (nabbaʾahā) of it, she said: Who informed you (anbaʾaka) of this? He said: The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me (nabbaʾanī)” [al-Taḥrīm 3] — he did not say anbaʾanī but turned to nabbaʾa, which is more emphatic, to point out that it was certain and came from Allah. Likewise His saying: “Allah has already informed us (nabbaʾanā) of your news” [al-Tawba 94], “then He will inform you (fa-yunabbiʾukum) of what you used to do” [al-Māʾida 105]. Prophethood (nubuwwa) is an embassy between Allah and those of His servants who have intellect, to remove their excuses in the matter of their Hereafter and their worldly life. The Prophet (al-nabī) is so called because he informs of what pure intellects find rest in. It can be on the pattern faʿīl meaning an agent (one who informs), because of His saying: “Inform (nabbiʾ) My servants” [al-Ḥijr 49], “Say: Shall I inform you” [Āl ʿImrān 15]; and it can mean the one acted upon (one who is informed), because of His saying: “The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me” [al-Taḥrīm 3]. Tanabbaʾa fulān means he claimed prophethood. By the original meaning of the language, the word should be usable of a true prophet, since it is the reflexive of nabbaʾa,
646-628-623|muf|6: like zayyanahu fa-tazayyana, ḥallāhu fa-taḥallā, jammalahu fa-tajammala. But since it became customary for those who falsely claim prophethood, its use for the truthful was avoided, and it is used only of one who fabricates his claim — as you say: tanabbaʾa Musaylima. In the diminutive of nabīʾ one says: Musaylima is a nubayyiʾ of evil — pointing out that his reports are not from Allah the Exalted's reports, as a man who heard his speech said: By Allah, this speech did not come from ill, that is: from Allah. And al-nabʾa is a faint sound.
646-628-623|lis|0: al-Nabaʾ is news (khabar); the plural is anbāʾ. “So-and-so has a nabaʾ” means a piece of news. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic: “About what are they asking one another? About the great news”
646-628-623|lis|1: — it is said [it refers to news] about the Qurʾān; and it is said, about the Resurrection; and it is said, about the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. Anbaʾahu iyyāhu and anbaʾahu bihi [he informed him of it], and likewise nabbaʾahu — taking its object with or without a preposition — meaning he told. Sībawayh reported: anā anbuʾuka [with u], by assimilation of vowels. And his saying:
639-638-645|maq|0: ʿAyn, ẓāʾ and mīm form one sound root indicating greatness and strength. al-ʿIẓam is the verbal noun of something great. You say ʿaẓuma, yaʿẓumu, ʿiẓaman [it became great], and ʿaẓẓamtuhu [I made it great / honoured it]. When something becomes great in your eyes you say aʿẓamtuhu and istaʿẓamtuhu. The muʿẓam of a thing is the greater part of it. The ʿaẓama of the forearm is its thick part. al-ʿAẓīma is a severe calamity that befalls. [The poet] said:
639-638-645|maq|1: [Poetry:] “If you escape it, you escape something of great calamity (ʿaẓīma) — otherwise I do not think you will escape.”
639-638-645|maq|2: Also from this root is al-ʿaẓm, the bone, which is well known; it was so called for its strength and hardness.
639-638-645|muf|0: al-ʿAẓm (bone), plural ʿiẓām. Allah the Exalted said: “bones, and We clothed the bones with flesh” [al-Muʾminūn 14] — and it is also read ʿaẓman in both places. From it the thick part of the forearm is called ʿaẓamat al-dhirāʿ, and the ʿaẓm of a saddle is its wooden frame without its straps. The original sense of ʿaẓuma al-shayʾ is: its bone became large. Then it was borrowed for everything large, and used in the same way whether the thing is perceived by the senses or by the mind, a physical thing or an idea. He said: “the punishment of a great (ʿaẓīm) Day” [al-Zumar 13], “Say: It is great news” [Ṣād 67], “About what are they asking one another? About the great news (al-nabaʾ al-ʿaẓīm)” [ʿAmma 1–2], “[a man] great from the two towns” [al-Zukhruf 31]. When ʿaẓīm is used of physical things, its basic use is for connected parts, while kathīr (many) is used for separate things; then ʿaẓīm may be said of separate things, as in a great army and great wealth, in the sense of much. And al-ʿaẓīma:
639-638-645|muf|1: is a calamity. al-Iʿẓāma and al-ʿiẓāma are something like a cushion with which a woman enlarges her hips.
639-638-645|lis|0: Among the attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is al-ʿAliyy al-ʿAẓīm (the Most High, the Most Great). The servant glorifies his Lord saying: Subḥāna rabbiya al-ʿaẓīm. al-ʿAẓīm is the One whose worth surpasses, and who is exalted above, the limits of intellects, so that encompassing His essence and reality cannot be conceived. ʿIẓam in the description of bodies is largeness in length, width and depth — and Allah the Exalted is far above that. The Prophet ﷺ said: “As for bowing (rukūʿ), magnify (ʿaẓẓimū) the Lord in it,” meaning: make Him in yourselves one possessing greatness. The greatness of Allah, glorified is He, is not described as to how, is not limited, and is not likened to anything. Servants must know that He is great as He described Himself and above that, without asking how and without limits. al-Layth said: al-ʿaẓama is self-aggrandisement, haughtiness and vanity. al-Azharī said: the greatness of Allah is not to be described as al-Layth described it; when a servant is described with ʿaẓama it is blame, because greatness in reality belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and a servant's ʿaẓama is his blameworthy pride and tyranny. In the ḥadīth:
639-638-645|lis|1: “Whoever magnifies himself in his own eyes will meet Allah, Blessed and Exalted, while He is angry [with him].”
639-638-645|lis|3: its origin. al-ʿIẓam is the opposite of smallness. ʿAẓuma, yaʿẓumu, ʿiẓaman and ʿaẓāmatan: it became large; it is ʿaẓīm and ʿuẓām. ʿIẓam al-amr: its greater part. Aʿẓamahu and istaʿẓamahu: he considered it great. Taʿāẓamahu: it was too great for him. “A matter that nothing taʿāẓamuhu”: nothing is great in comparison with it; and likewise a torrent that nothing taʿāẓamuhu. “Rain struck us that nothing taʿāẓamuhu”: nothing is great beside it. In the ḥadīth:
62e-644-641|maq|0: Khāʾ, lām and fāʾ have three roots: first, that something comes after something else and takes its place; second, the opposite of front; and third, change.
62e-644-641|maq|1: The first is al-khalf. al-Khalaf is what comes after. They say: he is a khalaf of truth from his father, and a khalf of evil from his father. When they mention neither truth nor evil they say khalaf for the good one and khalf for the bad. Allah the Exalted said: “Then there succeeded after them a [bad] succession (khalf)” [al-Aʿrāf 169]. al-Khillīfā is the caliphate (khilāfa); it was called khilāfa only because the second comes after the first, standing in his place. You say: I sat khilāfa so-and-so, i.e. after him. And al-khawālif in His saying: “They were content to be with those who stay behind (al-khawālif)” [al-Tawba 87]
62e-644-641|maq|2: are the women, because the men are away at their wars, raids and trading while the women remain behind them (yakhlufnahum) in the houses and dwellings. Hence one says: the tribe is khulūf, when the men are away and the women staying. In supplication they say “khalafa Allāhu ʿalayk,” meaning: may Allah be your successor [and guardian] for the father or close friend you have lost; and “akhlafa Allāhu lak,” meaning: may He give you in place of what went something that stands after it and replaces it. al-Khilfa is a plant that grows after the dry stubble; and the khilfa of trees is fruit that comes out after the [first] fruit. [The poet] said:
62e-644-641|maq|3: [Poetry:] “And she has, at al-Māṭirūn, when the ants have eaten what they gathered,
62e-644-641|maq|4: a second crop (khilfa) — until, when she has spent the spring there, she takes up residence among the churches of Jilliq.”
62e-644-641|maq|5: And Zuhayr said, in a line that confirms all we have mentioned:
62e-644-641|maq|6: [Poetry:] “In it the wild cows and white gazelles walk one after another (khilfa), while their young rise up from every resting place.”
62e-644-641|maq|7: He means: when these pass, those follow behind them.
62e-644-641|maq|8: Also from this root is al-khalf, drawing water, because those drawing water alternate, this one after that and that after this. [The poet] said about al-khalf:
62e-644-641|maq|9: [Poetry:] “For downy chicks like the young of the sandgrouse, whose water-fetcher (khalf) was slow in coming, too weak to rise, their crops reddish.”
62e-644-641|maq|10: One says akhlafa when he draws water.
62e-644-641|maq|11: The other root is khalf, which is the opposite of front. One says: this is behind me (khalfī) and this is in front of me. This is well known. Labīd said:
62e-644-641|maq|12: [Poetry:] “So she went off, thinking that each of the two openings — behind her and in front of her — was the place of danger.”
62e-644-641|maq|13: Also from this root is al-khilf, one of the teats of the udder; it was so called because it is behind the one after it.
62e-644-641|maq|14: As for the third, they say khalafa fūhu when [the smell of] his mouth changed, and akhlafa. This is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: “The changed breath (khulūf) of the fasting person's mouth is more fragrant with Allah than the scent of musk.” And from it is the saying of Ibn Aḥmar:
62e-644-641|maq|15: [Poetry:] “Youth has gone, life has changed (akhlafa), and brothers and time have turned strange.”
62e-644-641|maq|16: From it is breaking (khilāf) a promise. Khalafa al-rajul ʿan khuluq abīh: he changed from his father's character. al-Khalīf is said of a garment worn out in the middle, from which the worn part is taken out and then [the rest] sewn together; one says khalaftu al-thawb, akhlufuhu. This fits the measure both of this root and of the first.
62e-644-641|maq|17: One says: he promised me, fa-akhlaftuhu, i.e. I found that he had broken his promise to me. al-Aʿshā said:
62e-644-641|maq|18: [Poetry:] “He stayed, and cut his night short, so as to take provision — then he went on, and Qutayla broke (akhlafa) a promise.”
62e-644-641|maq|20: [Poetry:] “My two buckets are khilfān, and their two drawers too”
62e-644-641|maq|21: — it is because this one follows after that one. As for their saying: people differed (ikhtalafa) about such-and-such, and people are khilfa, i.e. differing — that is from the first root, because each of them sets aside his companion's view and puts himself in the place of the one he set aside. As for their calling the pregnant she-camel khalifa, it may be an exception to the root; or it may be stretched to say she brings forth young, and the young are a khalaf [successor] — but that is far-fetched. The plural of khalifa is al-makhāḍ, the pregnant ones.
62e-644-641|maq|22: Among what is exceptional to the three roots is al-khalīf, the path between two mountains. As for al-khālifa among the tent poles, perhaps it is at the back of the tent, and so belongs to the root of behind and front. Hence they say: so-and-so is the khālifa of his household, when he is not foremost among them.
62e-644-641|maq|23: From the root of change and corruption is the akhlaf camel, which walks on one side because of an ailment that afflicts it.
62e-644-641|muf|0: Khalf is the opposite of front. Allah the Exalted said: “He knows what is before them and what is behind them (khalfahum)” [al-Baqara 255], and the Exalted said: “For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him” [al-Raʿd 11], and the Exalted said: “Today We will save your body so that you may be a sign for those after you (khalfaka)” [Yūnus 92]. Khalf is the opposite of what goes before and precedes. One who comes later because of a deficiency in his rank is called khalf — hence it is said al-khalf is the worthless. One who comes later but not because of a lower rank is called khalaf. The Exalted said: “Then there succeeded after them a [bad] succession (khalf)” [al-Aʿrāf 169]. And it was said: he kept silent a thousand [times] and then spoke
62e-644-641|muf|1: [Poetry:] “… and they gave you longing as provision, whichever way they went.”
62e-644-641|muf|2: a khalf — i.e. worthless speech. The backside, when wind comes out of it, is called khalfa; and so is one whose speech is corrupt or who is corrupt in himself. One says: takhallafa fulānun fulānan:
62e-644-641|muf|3: when he stayed behind him, and when he came after another, and when he took his place; its verbal noun is al-khilāfa with kasra. Khalufa khalāfatan with fatḥa: he became corrupt, so he is khālif, i.e. worthless and foolish. The worthless is expressed by khalf, as in: “Then there succeeded after them a [bad] succession who neglected prayer” [Maryam 59]. One who succeeds another and fills his place is called khalaf. al-Khilfa is said of each one succeeding the other. The Exalted said: “It is He who made the night and the day in succession (khilfa)” [al-Furqān 62]. And it is said: their affair is khilfa, i.e. part of it comes after part. The poet said:
62e-644-641|muf|4: [Editor's numbering of the poetry citation: no. 148]
62e-644-641|muf|5: “In it the wild cows and white gazelles walk one after another (khilfa).” Aṣābathu khilfa is a euphemism for diarrhoea and frequent going [to relieve oneself]. Khalafa fulānun fulānan: he undertook the matter on his behalf, either with him or after him. The Exalted said: “And if We willed, We could have made among you angels succeeding [one another] on earth” [al-Zukhruf 60]. al-Khilāfa is acting on another's behalf, either because the one represented is absent, or has died, or is unable, or to honour the one appointed as successor. In this last sense Allah made His friends successors on earth. The Exalted said: “It is He who made you successors (khalāʾif) on earth” [Fāṭir 39], “It is He who made you successors of the earth” [al-Anʿām 165], and He said: “And my Lord will bring another people to succeed you” [Hūd 57]. Khalāʾif is the plural of khalīfa, and khulafāʾ the plural of khalīf. The Exalted said: “O Dāwūd, We have made you a successor (khalīfa) on earth” [Ṣād 26], “And We made them successors” [Yūnus 73], “He made you successors after the people of Nūḥ” [al-Aʿrāf 69]. al-Ikhtilāf and al-mukhālafa are that each takes a path other than the other's in his state or his speech. Khilāf (difference) is more general than ḍidd (opposite), because every two opposites differ, but not every two things that differ are opposites. Since differing among people in speech can lead to dispute, it was borrowed for dispute and argument. He said:
